findings.title: Adding abstract `order()` breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: `order()` is added as an abstract method to the public `CryptoProvider` SPI. Existing third-party or downstream `CryptoProvider` implementations compiled against the previous `keycloak-common` do not implement it, and `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider()` now invokes `CryptoProvider::order` on every provider discovered via `ServiceLoader`. Those implementations will fail with `AbstractMethodError` during initialization, turning a previously valid provider into a startup failure. Make `order()` a default method with a sensible default priority, or explicitly handle providers that do not implement it.

findings.title: Provider selection is nondeterministic when real providers have equal priority
findings.body: `detectProvider()` now silently chooses the highest-priority provider, but all existing real providers added in this PR (`DefaultCryptoProvider`, `FIPS1402Provider`, and `WildFlyElytronProvider`) return the same `order()` value of 200. If more than one of them is present on the classpath, the winner depends on `ServiceLoader` iteration/classpath order. In particular, a FIPS deployment that also sees the default provider can silently fall back to non-FIPS crypto instead of failing closed as the old multi-provider check did. Assign distinct priorities to the real security providers, or reject ties involving security-sensitive providers.

findings.title: `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the default KeyStore provider, not BouncyCastle
findings.body: The `CryptoProvider` contract says `getBouncyCastleProvider()` returns the non-FIPS or FIPS BouncyCastle security provider. This implementation instead creates a default `KeyStore` and returns its provider, which is normally `SUN`/`SunJSSE`, not BC or BCFIPS. Any caller relying on this method to obtain BouncyCastle will receive an unrelated provider and may fail cryptically or make incorrect security assumptions. Return the actual BC provider if one is available, or throw `UnsupportedOperationException` rather than returning a different provider.

findings.title: New provider-selection behavior is not tested
findings.body: The added test only round-trips ASN.1 ECDSA signatures through the new encoder/decoder. It does not test the central new behavior: loading `AuthzClientCryptoProvider` via `META-INF/services`, or verifying that `CryptoIntegration` chooses the higher-priority `DefaultCryptoProvider` when both providers are on the classpath. A regression in the sorting/selection logic could therefore pass CI. Additionally, the ES384/ES512 cases use the default 256-bit EC key, so they do not actually exercise P-384/P-521 keys.
